content: Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMSF) is the most severe tick-borne rickettsial illness in the United States. It is caused by infection with the bacterial organism Rickettsia rickettsii. Symptoms of Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever Patients infected with R. rickettsii typically seek medical attention during the first week of illness, following an incubation period of approximately 5 to 10 days after a tick bite. The early clinical presentation of RMSF is often nonspecific and may mimic other infectious or non-infectious diseases. Initial symptoms may include: Fever Nausea Vomiting Muscle pain Loss of appetite Severe headache As the disease progresses, later signs and symptoms may include: Rash Abdominal pain Joint pain Diarrhea Three key components of the clinical presentation are fever, rash, and a history of a tick bite. However, one or more of these components may not be present when the patient first seeks medical care. RMSF can be a severe illness, and most patients require hospitalization. Causes of Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever RMSF is transmitted through the bite of an infected tick. The primary tick vectors in the United States are the American dog tick (Dermacentor variabilis) and the Rocky Mountain wood tick (Dermacentor andersoni). The brown dog tick (Rhipicephalus sanguineus) has also been implicated as a vector, as well as the tick Amblyomma cajennense in countries south of the United States. Risk Factors for Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever The highest frequency of reported RMSF cases occurs among males, Caucasians, and children. Two-thirds of cases occur in children under the age of 15, with the peak age being 5 to 9 years old. Individuals with frequent exposure to dogs and those living near wooded areas or areas with high grass are at increased risk of infection. RMSF is a seasonal disease, occurring most commonly in the United States from April through September. The highest incidence rates have been reported in North Carolina and Oklahoma. Although the disease was first discovered in the Rocky Mountain region, relatively few cases are reported from that area today. Diagnosis of Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever The diagnosis of RMSF is based on a combination of clinical signs and symptoms and specialized confirmatory laboratory tests. Common laboratory findings suggestive of RMSF include: Thrombocytopenia (low platelet count) Hyponatremia (low blood sodium levels) Elevated liver enzyme levels When to Seek Urgent Medical Care Contact your healthcare provider if symptoms such as fever and rash occur after exposure to ticks or following a known tick bite. Untreated RMSF can lead to life-threatening complications. Treatment Options for Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever RMSF is best treated with a tetracycline antibiotic, usually doxycycline. The recommended dosage is 100 mg every 12 hours for adults or 4 mg/kg body weight per day in two divided doses for children under 45 kg (100 lbs). Treatment should continue for at least 3 days after the fever subsides and until there is evidence of clinical improvement. The standard duration of treatment is 5 to 10 days. Since laboratory confirmation is generally not available during the acute phase of illness, treatment is initiated based on clinical and epidemiological information. Diseases with Similar Symptoms to Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever Other diseases that may present with similar symptoms include: Babesiosis (Babesia infection) Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever Diseases related to insects and their relatives Lyme disease Southern tick-associated rash illness (STARI) Tick-borne relapsing fever Prevention of Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever Reducing exposure to ticks decreases the likelihood of infection with tick-borne diseases. For individuals exposed to tick-infested habitats, prompt and careful inspection and removal of crawling or attached ticks is an important preventive measure. Extended attachment time may be required before organisms are transmitted from the tick to the host. While it is unreasonable to completely avoid activities that may result in tick exposure, the following precautions can help protect against tick bites: Wear light-colored clothing to make ticks easier to spot. Tuck pant legs into socks to prevent ticks from crawling up inside pants. Apply repellents to discourage tick attachment. Permethrin-based repellents can be sprayed on boots and clothing and remain effective for several days. DEET-based repellents can be applied to the skin but require reapplication after a few hours. Use DEET with caution on children. Conduct a full-body check after returning from potentially tick-infested areas, using a mirror to inspect all parts of the body. Remove any ticks found on the body. Check children for ticks, especially in the hair, after returning from such areas. Ticks may also be carried into the household on clothing and pets, so both should be carefully examined to exclude ticks. Prognosis for Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever Treatment usually cures the infection. Complications are rare but can include paralysis, hearing loss, nerve damage, and, in rare cases, death. RMSF can be a severe illness, and most patients require hospitalization. Infection with R. rickettsii is thought to provide long-lasting immunity against reinfection. However, prior illness with RMSF should not deter individuals from practicing good tick-preventive measures or seeking medical attention if symptoms consistent with RMSF occur, especially following a tick bite, as other diseases may also be transmitted by ticks.
